items.title: Pricing Symbolic Rules by What GNNs Leave Unlearned
items.summary: Symbolic knowledge (motif counts, ring counts, label constraints) is routinely added to graph neural networks (GNNs) and justified by their limited expressivity. We replace this yardstick with an exact one. The largest log-loss reduction a rule $S$ can give a model family is $I(Y;S\midσ)$ given what the family computes; every realised gain splits exactly into this term plus repaid neural debt; and for a trained network with representation $T$ the value is $I(Y;S\mid T)$, the label information training failed to extract. Rule design thus becomes rule discovery: we score candidates on the network's out-of-fold residual against calibrated permutation nulls with family-wise error control. On ZINC, discovery recovers the hidden ring term $\max(0,\ell_{\max}-6)$ of the target in three independent runs ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.001$) and beats expert cycle counts; frozen and applied to five unseen datasets it is never significantly worse than the plain network or the expert rule, and on BBBP it significantly beats both.

items.title: Reconstructing hourly traffic on every street of a capital from a sparse counting network: a graph neural network applied to Paris
items.summary: Micro-scale air quality models require hourly traffic data on every road segment, whereas permanent counters cover only a small part of the network. A graph neural network (GNN) was developed to reconstruct hourly traffic flows on the 32,163 road segments of Paris intra-muros from the 1,573 segments equipped with a counter (4.9%). The model adapts the Graph Neural Network for Urban Interpolation (GNNUI) to a real, sparse counting network. Flows are decoded on the edges of the junction graph (one edge per segment, both directions summed), a traffic climatology serves as an offset in a zero-inflated negative-binomial likelihood, and training proceeds by masking counters. Eight-fold spatial cross-validation, with counters sharing a published series merged before splitting, distinguishes interpolation at a withheld counter in an instrumented district (R${}^2$ = 0.89, error of a quarter of the mean flow) from extrapolation to a district without counters (R${}^2$ = 0.74, a third of the mean flow). These scores hold on main axes where counters are located, while relative errors are about 50% on the few counted local streets. Ablations show that the climatology offset tends to help extrapolation. Road attributes, time cycles and the live state of the counting network matter most, while weather inputs have no significant effect. The masking rate is the only inherited hyperparameter with a clear effect. When evaluated on January--August 2026 (outside the training period), the frozen model stayed around the error band of previous years.

items.title: Graph RAG Explained: How Knowledge Graphs Improve AI Retrieval | Coursera
items.summary:
GraphRAG is an advanced type of retrieval augmented generation (RAG) that uses knowledge graphs to map and extract data points and their relationships. Traditional vector-based RAG systems retrieve text fragments based on semantic similarity with the search query, often failing to capture the context and relationships between entities. While large language models (LLMs) based on traditional RAG systems excel at retrieving specific information from relevant knowledge sources, they often struggle [...] GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph by extracting entities and their relationships from multiple data sources and storing them as connected nodes and edges; it retrieves relevant subgraphs upon query and injects that structured context into LLM prompts to produce more accurate responses. [...] ## How does GraphRAG work?

The GraphRAG process first entails collecting information from diverse data sources and processing it with an LLM to extract entities and their relationships. Using a graph database tool, you map entities as nodes and relationships as edges, add detailed contextual information, and store the graph in a database like Neo4j or AWS Neptune.

items.title: Building Open Intelligence Infrastructure: GraphRAG, Neo4j, and Decentralized GPUs on Nosana
items.summary:
GraphRAG allows language models to retrieve contextual information from a knowledge graph before generating an answer. Instead of relying exclusively on information embedded in a model's training data, the system can reason over an external, structured information environment.

Our objective is to make this process useful for real-world investigations involving public information.

## Experimenting with GraphRAG on decentralized GPUs [...] Information is fragmented. Relationships are difficult to identify. Investigations often require substantial time, technical expertise, and computational resources.

We believe that combining knowledge graphs, open-source AI, and decentralized computing can help reduce these barriers.

Neo4j provides the relational foundation. GraphRAG provides a mechanism for contextual retrieval and reasoning. Nosana provides an alternative computational infrastructure. [...] Neo4j for knowledge graph construction and relationship modeling.
 GraphRAG for retrieving and reasoning over interconnected information.
 Nosana for decentralized GPU computing and the execution of open-source AI models.

Rather than treating these technologies as separate components, we are investigating how they can operate as a unified pipeline.

## Why knowledge graphs matter for public intelligence

Large public datasets are difficult to investigate because information is fragmented.

items.title: Neo4j's Nyah Macklin: Vector RAG Fails at Counting; Knowledge Graphs Give AI a Paper Trail — BigGo Finance
items.summary:
### A Map for Machine-Readable Context

Macklin's definition of GraphRAG is precise: it is RAG where the retrieval path includes a knowledge graph. The contrast is architectural, not cosmetic. In a standard pipeline, text lands in a vector index. In GraphRAG, a graph sits between the query and the answer. [...] That is where GraphRAG enters. The architecture keeps the vector layer but adds a knowledge graph directly into the retrieval path. Instead of just fetching similar chunks, the agent can traverse from node to node through typed relationships — and reconstruct the path it took. For Macklin, this is the answer to AI's "black box" problem in regulated domains. "Nobody wants vibe banking," she said. "You don't want your agent just having access to your money and then spending all of your money." [...] Vector-only retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) breaks down on questions requiring multi-hop reasoning, aggregation, or traceable provenance, argues Nyah Macklin, senior software engineer and developer advocate at Neo4j. Speaking on the AI Engineer podcast, Macklin demonstrates that the fix is GraphRAG — an architecture that keeps the vector layer but adds a knowledge graph to the retrieval path so an agent can traverse typed relationships and explain how it reached an answer.
